messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sarah met her husband, Ben, in her final year of high school, and they married just after graduation. She had imagined a life filled with small joys: finding a part-time job at the local library, taking art classes, and saving up for a small apartment of their own. That was seven months ago, before the world she knew was dismantled in the space of a few minutes. She had been walking home from a friend's house one evening, taking a familiar shortcut through a quiet residential street. The sudden, guttural roar of a motorcycle tore through the stillness, and before she could turn, it was beside her. The man smelled so strongly of liquor it was like a physical blow. He grabbed her arm, his words a torrent of angry, guttural sounds she didn't understand but later learned was Arabic. The assault itself is a sequence of disjointed sensory snapshots: the smell of stale whiskey, the rough texture of his jacket, the terrifying sound of his shouting.

In the weeks that followed, the world outside her front door became a landscape of potential threats. She stopped going out after dark entirely, a decision that felt less like a choice and more like a basic survival instinct. Her part-time job search dwindled to nothing; the thought of interviews, of being in new places, was unbearable. Now unemployed, she spends most days inside the small house she shares with Ben, but even here, there is no peace. Every creak of the floorboards, every rattle of the windowpane, is the sound of an intruder. She finds herself listening constantly, her body coiled tight, waiting for a danger she is certain is about to arrive. When she does venture out for groceries, she walks with her head on a swivel, constantly checking over her shoulder for footsteps that are never there. She had come to believe that safety was an illusion, a story people told themselves, and that she was one of the few who now knew the terrible truth.

The past is not past for Sarah; it is a living presence. The sound of any motorcycle, even one blocks away, can instantly bring the entire event back with a force that steals her breath. In those moments, she is no longer in her living room but back on that dark pavement. She can hear his shouting in her ears as clearly as if he were standing beside her, and the phantom smell of alcohol fills her nostrils, so real it makes her gag. Last week, Ben was watching an action movie when a motorcycle chase scene came on. Sarah screamed and scrambled into a corner of the sofa, her hands over her ears, acting as if she were fending off an attacker. Ben shut off the television, but it took nearly an hour for her trembling to subside.

She has also become a stranger to her own body. Showers are taken in near darkness, and she avoids looking at her reflection in the mirror, dressing quickly in oversized sweaters and loose pants. It feels as though her body is no longer hers, but a piece of evidence from a crime scene, a constant, physical reminder of her own failure. This is the thought that circles endlessly: somebody else would have stopped it. A stronger woman would have fought back, a smarter woman would have screamed sooner, a better woman wouldn't have been walking down that street at all. This conviction has hollowed her out, leaving behind the belief that she is no longer capable of being the person she was. The girl who loved to paint, who laughed easily with her friends, who was excited about her future with her new husband—that person is gone, replaced by this fragile, terrified ghost. The approaching one-year anniversary of the assault looms in her calendar, a date she avoids thinking about but can feel getting closer each day. It was the dread of that day, and the quiet desperation in Ben’s eyes, that finally pushed her to seek help. She is terrified that this is all she will ever be, but a small, flickering part of her hopes that she might one day learn how to live in the world again.
